analysis.one_liner: Repeals the individual alternative minimum tax and lets taxpayers opt into a simplified two-rate income tax.
analysis.headline: Paul Ryan's bill to repeal the individual AMT and offer an optional 10% and 25% income tax was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on January 28, 2009 and never received a markup or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out the alternative minimum tax for individuals and let any taxpayer permanently switch into a stripped-down income tax with just two rates: 10% on income up to $50,000 for singles ($100,000 for couples) and 25% above that, with no itemized deductions like mortgage interest or charitable giving. It would also make the 15% tax rate on capital gains and dividends permanent rather than letting it expire. Sponsors pitched it as a simpler, fairer tax code; the rate structure and the locked-in investment tax break would cut taxes most for people with the largest incomes.
analysis.who_benefits: Middle-income filers with simple returns would owe less and file simpler forms under the optional 10%/25% system. But the largest dollar gains would go to high-income households: the top rate would drop from 35% to 25%, and the 15% rate on capital gains and dividends would be made permanent.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners and investors, plus simple-return filers

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the alternative minimum tax on individual taxpayers for tax years beginning after 2008, ending a parallel tax system that had been pulling more middle- and upper-middle-income households into higher bills each year.

Taxpayers could elect a simplified system with a 10% rate up to $50,000 of income for singles ($100,000 for joint filers) and 25% above that, keeping only personal exemptions, a $3,500 per-dependent allowance, and a $12,500 ($25,000 joint) standard deduction instead of itemized deductions.
The bill makes permanent the 15% maximum rate on capital gains and dividends enacted under the 2003 tax law, rather than letting that rate reduction expire.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — the AMT repeal, the lower 25% top rate, and permanent investment tax rates all reduce revenue with no offset anywhere in the bill, meaning larger deficits or future pressure on spending. Households that currently benefit from itemized deductions (mortgage interest, state and local taxes, charitable gifts) would owe more than under current law if they switched to the flat system.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Treasury, and households that itemize deductions

drawbacks.text: The rate structure is a large unpaid-for tax cut tilted to the top: the top rate falls from the up-to-35% rates then in effect to 25%, and the 15% capital gains and dividends rate becomes permanent, while the bill contains no revenue offset.

The election is largely irrevocable: a taxpayer can reverse it only once, and otherwise only after marriage, divorce, or death, so a family whose circumstances change in other ways — a new child, a home purchase, a layoff — could be locked into a system that no longer fits them.

Simplification comes at the price of deductions many households use, including mortgage interest and charitable giving, which housing charities and similar interests in the regular tax code would lose value if large numbers of filers switched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The simplification and AMT repeal are real, and millions of households with uncomplicated returns would have come out ahead. But the bill's largest effects by dollar value are the 25% top rate and the permanent 15% investment rate, which concentrate their gains among the highest earners and add to deficits without any pay-for. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that this is a major tax cut for the top of the income scale wrapped around a genuine simplification offer.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 111th Congress ended without ever getting a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Ryan (R-WI) introduced the Taxpayer Choice Act of 2009 in the House on January 28, 2009, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
Twenty-two House Republicans cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list contains no Democrats.
The action history shows no activity beyond the initial referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action — through the end of the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained directly, because the bill never moved and the tax code stayed as it was. The clearest beneficiaries of the outcome were whoever would have borne the cost of the bill's unpaid-for tax cuts, though Congress separately extended the expiring investment tax rates before the end of 2010.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the tax code stayed unchanged

for.name: Rep. Paul Ryan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited original cosponsors from the Republican side of the House.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Tax-writing committee with jurisdiction over the bill; chaired by a Democrat in this Congress
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans in a House with 253 Democrats and 178 Republicans; no Democrat signed on and no roll call was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill cuts the top individual rate from 35% to 25% and makes the 15% capital gains and dividends rate permanent, so the largest dollar savings go to those with the biggest incomes and investment gains. The revenue loss is unfunded, leaving the cost to deficits or future spending cuts that fall on everyone else.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: An optional two-rate system with no itemized deductions would mean far simpler returns for filers who opt in, cutting demand for paid preparation and software. The regular system would remain for anyone who stays out.
